title: Competitive Innovations in the Mortal Realms: 2026-11-04
content:
Welcome to Competitive Innovations, our weekly feature for a number of game lines across the tabletop wargame space. Each week our army list and tactics experts canvass the top tournaments for their game of specialty, looking at the week’s top match-ups and how they played out on the tabletop to let you know what’s hot, what’s not, and what might be coming next as the competitive meta evolves year-round.

A bit smaller this week, but a nice mix-up from our usual countries in comp innovations, as we head to Scandinavia and Central America for two GTs.

This Week's Events

  • 2D6 Carnage 2026 - Norway
  • Warhammex GT Open 2 - Mexico

Thoughts

SCE Annihilators lists are a bit of a mixed bag. They drop down, and try and make their charges. If they make it, they will probably pick up whatever they went into, if they don't, they just stand there impotently while the enemy either picks them off or just keeps their distance.

The score seems to imply it was a bit mixed. not a complete blow out, with Praetors and Reclusians to back them up they're not completely without damage options if they fail, but the mobility of this kind of Lumineth list means that they are very difficult to lock down for Stormcast, with their slower walk speed once they've hit the ground.

Result

The List

See Showdown

Archetype

Thoughts

Severith and and the Hurakan Spirit of the Wind make a great synergy with the wind chargers. Thanks to Severith's ability to buff other Hurakan units, they can get -1 to be hit, and extra 6" of movement and +5 control out of the gate. This means these guys are fast and hard to lock down. If they get into combat, Severith can inflict -1 to wound and the generic spirit Strike Last, making them east pickings for some of the stronger beat sticks in the army.

Light of Eltharion and Ellania and Elathor (When Elathor is in charge) are brutal combat pieces who can swing in and pick up a lot of impressive threats. The Riverblades hang back as objective grabbers and assassin pieces, while the Wardens guard the Heroes from a frontal attack.

The Best of the Rest

There were 5 more players on 4-1 records. They were:

  • 2nd - Tomasz Mucha - Sylvaneth: Belthanos, Drycha and Kurnoths.
  • 3rd - Damian Grzybek - Disciples of Tzeentch:Lord of Change with mixed infantry and a Daemon Prince.
  • 4th - Michal Pisarski - Stormcast Eternals: See Showdown.
  • 5th - Ole Vatland - Helsmiths of Hashut: Urak-Taar and Daemonsmith on Bull with Sentinels and artillery.
  • 6th - Andrii Yefremenkov - Kruleboyz: Gobbsprakk and Rippa Vulcha with various monsters.

Thoughts

Honestly, no contest here. The Kharadrons simply don't really have an obvious targets to go after and a Darkoath list creates a massive number of wounds to try and carve through and very few armies can muster that much damage.

Matt clears this pretty handedly, creating an impenetrable wall of chaff with his disposable Darkoaths and then clapping back with his more heavily armed pieces.

Result

Slaves to Darkness Victory - 80 - 36

Matt Nguyen - Slaves to Darkness - 1st Place

Darkoath Warqueen. Credit: SRM

The List

See Showdown

Archetype

Darkoaths

Thoughts

This time I don't really need to give my thoughts because I was able to get it directly from Matt himself how the list works:

"Hey everyone! My name is Matt "Noog" Nguyen and I'm the pilot of this Darkoath STD list. As an ex-BOC player, I wanted to find a playstyle that was similar to the 2nd or 3rd edition book. Thankfully, I've found that with the Darkoath half of STD. The core identity of the Darkoath list is to overwhelm the opponent with MSU waves of trash, combat pieces that can trade up, and being able to play a 5 turn game where the opponent will struggle to stop me from dominating primary + achieving most of my battle tactics. What makes this list work starting off is the subfaction Darkoath Horde. For one CP during my movement phase, I can revive any non-hero Darkoath unit like Marauders, Savagers, and even Wilderfiends to come wholly within 6 of a board edge outside of 3 of enemy units. This ensures that no back objectives or foot heroes are safe from being assailed.

The bread and butter of the list lies in Darkoath Marauders and Wilderfiends. Having 5 units of MSU marauders not only lets me have layers of screens for my army and roll 50+ dice on death to do mortals on a 5+, but they also serve as batteries for the Wilderfiends. If any models die within 12 of a Wilderfiend, they can charge up sacrifice points. With up to 6 sacrifice points, they can use it to turn off commands on a 5+, do mortals on a 3+, or heal themselves. The amount of utility, tankiness, and damage for a 120 point unit makes bringing 3 worthwhile as they are an MSU threat that cannot be ignored by your opponent.

Leading these vast hordes are seven heroes in the list. The Darkoath Chieftain can chain-fight to give +1 attacks to efficient combat units like Savagers while the Darkoath Warqueen can potentially give out a 5+ ward on an objective she's contesting to any Darkoath on it. Gunnar brand and Singri are used in the list to help score Burning for Vengeance 1 and Siege of Ashes 1 or farm places of power. The Oathsworn Kin are my 1 cast in the list whose job is to play behind the army to get ready to cast 3D6 charge or fight last. If need be, they can often be sent in as a trading piece. The Chaos Lord sits by the Scourge of Asqhy Warriors to chain fight them for +1 to wound. Finally, we have the Ogroid Myrmidon with both of my command trait and artifact. For an 120 point unit, he can get up to 12-15 attacks with Rune of Murder on 3s and 2s rend 1 3 damage each and be able to fight twice with Deathmonger. This creates an insane combat hero that will always uptrade for his cost. I've had him kill the Shadow Queen, Redd, 10 gluttons, and other expensive units in one go. All of my heroes are just layers to this onion that is my list.

The mainline hammers of the list are my reinforced block of 20 Savagers and my Scourge of Aqshy Chaos Warriors. Now that they have allowed most Warcry units to become reinforceable, a block of reinforced Savagers at 180 points is an insane potential hammer. Starting off at 2 attacks each at 4s 3s crit mortals 1 damage each, they can be given Mark of Khorne for +1 attacks and if the Darkoath Chieftain chain-fights them, then they go up to 81 attacks with crit mortals. The most critical part of my list however is my reinforced Scourge of Aqshy Chaos Warriors. While everything else is a 4-5+ save in the army, they are my anvil and hammer in this list. Equipping them with Dread Banner lets them stop commands with any foe they are in combat with which stops all out defense and power through so your opponent's units are forced to stay in the mud with them. The Warriors also become the strongest combat piece in the army when they get to 7 fury which gives them +1 damage to their melee attacks and strike first as long as they don't charge. 40 wounds on a 3+ save and Mark of Khorne to get them to 3 attacks each at potentially damage 2 has turned the tide in my practice and GT games. I've watched them solo Ogor, DOK, and other strong combat armies.

All of my screens, trading pieces, MSU units, and hammers in the list lets the army be at 190+ wounds. The wound density lets me absorb double turns from my opponents and not care about turn priority as most other armies would. Every single warscroll in this list has a job to do whenever it is to die for the glory of the Chaos Gods to help me waylay my opponents or embark on the Path of Glory to earn their recognition of their dark deities by slaying the most powerful of my opponent's units. Every single unit is expendable and I have often sacrificed my heroes and deadliest hammers in order to dominate primary and tactics. At its heart, the list is a board control army that has built in recursion, lots of MSU to cause confusion for my opponents on what units they should target, and cheap combat units that will always trade up into expensive reinforced hammers or god monsters while letting me play a 5 turn game of Age of Sigmar."

The Best of the Rest

There was 2 more player on 4-1 records. They were:

  • 2nd - Eduardo Rodriguez - Daughters of Khaine: Morathi and Mixed Infantry.
  • 3rd - Luis Mendoza - Sylvaneth: Herohammer with Belthanos, Drycha, Spirit of Durthu and Treelord Ancient.

title: BattleTech Mech Overview: JagerMech and JagerMech III
content:
Today, MechWarriors, we are cancelling the apocalypse!

Or, well, today we're talking about the usually-65-ton JagerMech. Some of its variants might be capable of cancelling a small apocalypse. We've got Abomination creation rules now, we could put this theorem to the test...

Lyran Commonwealth Jagermech. Credit: SRM

One of the multiple Star-League-era efforts to address the flaws of the Rifleman, the JagerMech is Kallon's own second bite at that apple. It's very close to being the same mech, down to utilizing the same Garret D2j targeting and tracking system (with the Anti-Aircraft Targeting Quirk that comes with it), but it's usually five tons heavier (we'll... we'll get there) and usually mitigates the Rifleman's heat issues by leaning further into ammunition-dependent weapons.

On the one hand, this means that it's usually a thinly-armored mech stuffed with explosive crits.

On the other hand, this means that it's usually extremely cheap.

Which hand wins? Well, let's take a look!

Variants

These mechs have all been reviewed based on a standard F through S scale, which you can find described on our landing page here (along with all of our other ‘Mech reviews, the name of the box you can buy to get any of the mechs we have covered, and our general methodology).

JM6-A

BattleTech model numbers are made up and the points don't matter, so the "A" is not the first in-universe variant, but it does date to the Star League. It forms a little sub-clade of its own alongside the JM6-B as "the ones that have LRMs on them," namely an LRM-15 in each arm a la Catapult. The A pairs its missile launchers with an AC/2 in each arm, and one medium laser in each side torso strives valiantly to divert critical hits away from the spicy ammo slots (one ton AC and one LRM in the left torso and a second ton of LRMs in the right torso).

The JM6-A doesn't jump (moving 4/6/0)  and doesn't have anything beyond the base ten single heat sinks, but the autocannons are still heavy enough to stop it two tons short of the Catapult C1's armor coverage. 17/20/17 across the front torsos is passable, if not ideal, but its rear coverage is a dismal 3/5/3, and it only has 16 pips on each leg and 11 on the arms. Heat's okay; 2+ movement firing the long range guns, neutral at a run firing the ACs and the MLs, and -2 at a run firing just the MLs.

1,122 BV is cheap, though, 277 BV cheaper than the aforementioned Catapult C1 (and even a little bit cheaper than a Trebuchet 5N!), and this mech has great range. Within the specific context of "I am way in the backfield providing fire support for a larger force," this isn't bad, but that's not really the BattleTech most of us are playing, and dear lord this mech is allergic to being within six hexes of its opposition.

Lynn's Rating: D+.

JM6-B

Oh no, they made it worse. The -B is exactly the JM6-A except it swaps the AC/2s and their ton of ammo for a pair of Large Lasers and a wholly inadequate +3 heat sinks.

This mech builds 3+ Movement heat firing the Large Lasers alone. 9+ Movement firing all the lasers. If you wanted to fire the missiles and the large lasers together, that's 13+ Movement. I'm not even going to address the possibility of an Alpha Strike.

And this costs 1,248 BV?

Weren't we trying to fix the Rifleman's heat problems here, Kallon?

Shameful.

Lynn's Rating: F.

JM6-DD

Jumping ahead to the Helm Renaissance, the DD is... hm.  I'm going to call it an interesting value proposition, though the JM6-DDa, its Jihad-era refit, overshadows it in that regard. The DD uses an XL engine (still 260-rated for the JagerMech's usual 4/6/0 profile) to buy tonnage to pack an AC/2 and a UAC/5 in each arm, a ton of ammo for each gun, CASE which actually matters now with the Core Rules update, and a medium pulse laser in each side torso. Ten single heat sinks are honestly enough for that as long as you don't take an engine crit, with even a full alpha strike being plausible if a shot somehow lined up for one (though the poor range compatibility of the AC/2s and the MPLs makes that unlikely).

The Double D's Ferro-Fibrous armor coat is thinner than the A and B's armor, but it's been redistributed to keep decent protection on the torso (17/18/17 across the front and an improved 5/5/5 across the back) and full coverage on the head while sacrificing the limbs, with just 12 armor pips on each leg and eight on each arm. Each arm has 18 HP total.

The major value here is cost-effectiveness. A stiff breeze can threaten the DD, but it only costs 965 BV, and what you get for that is the potential for a PSR's worth of damage with good range, added together from a set of guns which looks piddly enough your opponent will likely underestimate them, backed by an okay close-range bite if anything tries to dive it. Make no mistake, this is nowhere close to a world-beater, but it is dirt cheap for what it is, and that's its own value.

Lynn's Rating: C is for cheap.

JM6-DDa

What I just said about the DD's cost-effectiveness?

Yeah, let's double down on that.

The DDa swaps the DD's armament for LAC/2s (two tons of ammo), AC/5s (three tons of ammo), regular Medium Lasers (moved to the CT) and a targeting computer. The ACs are happy flinging AP and Precision both (and you can even feed the AC/5s some flak ammo on top, as a treat, if you need to actually shoot at planes), their range bands line up perfectly (except for the AC/5s having a minimum), the DDa only builds movement heat on an alpha strike even with its 10 SHS, accuracy is improved on all the guns, and the BV?

The BV goes down. This sets you back 911 BV.

This is still a slow mech with terrible armor, but the value proposition it represents is phenomenal, and the Core changes have only made it better. Pressure your opponent with a scary frontline to distract them and you can absolutely make your investment back from this mech.

Lynn's Rating: B is for budget.

1st Federated Suns Armored Cavalry JagerMech. Credit: Valk.

JM6-DG

Remember the Avatar OG? We like the Avatar OG. The "Double Gauss" JagerMech takes the exact same weaponry as the Avatar OG (plus an extra two tons of ammo it won't live long enough to need) and shoves it into the chassis of a JM6-DD. At 1,625 BV, this only saves 150 BV relative to the Avatar OG, and it trades away seventy-six pips of armor to get there.

The JM6-DG wants you to think it's the minimum viable caddy for twin gauss rifles. This is a lie. It is below minimum. Take a Galahad 2D. Take a Sun Cobra. Take the Avatar OG. Take a friggin tank; if you don't need mobility you can get three Gauss Rifles with a targeting computer on the DI Morgan (Gauss) and save four BV over the JagerMech DG.

Just don't take a JagerMech DG. 1,625 BV is too much to pay for one-shot gauss rifles, and it's not likely to live long enough to shoot twice.

Lynn's Rating: F+.

JM6-DGr

Take a JM6-DG. Give it double heat sinks. Swap the medium lasers to ERMLs. That's the DGr. It goes up to 1,661 BV and has gained absolutely no survivability.

These mechs could have carried less ammunition and had more armor. They could have dropped the medium lasers and had more armor. They could've done Galahad cosplay and shrunk the engine and had more armor.

Instead, they decided that valuable weapons with explosive capacitors should be put in arms as well-armored as an Ostsol's.

Shameful display.

Lynn's Rating: F.

JM6-H

Okay, after those DGs I need something to pick my spirits up, I need something...

Bah Gawd, that's the Marian Hegemony's music!

Heck yeah, we've got a funny rocket launcher variant, and more than that, it's a... shockingly competently designed rocket launcher variant?

The JagerMech Haitch mounts an LB 2-X and a Large Laser in each arm, and can sink all their heat at a run with ten Double Heat Sinks. Three Rocket Launcher 15s in each side torso give it a dramatic, if inaccurate, close-in punch, and it still has enough tonnage for the thickest coat of Ferro-Fibrous we've yet seen on a JagerMech, 24/29/24 and 5/7/5 pips of armor on the front and rear side torsos, 16 on the arms, 22 on the legs. As a further benefit, unexpended rocket launchers apparently don't explode when crit, and expended rocket launchers still soak crits, so the side torsos are hilariously well-padded, even without CASE on the LB ammo.

It's not all upside here: The H only carries one ton of LB 2-X ammo, so you need to choose between being able to make flak attacks and being able to consistently hit PSR-threshold damage output, and the range bands are a bit fiddly on the arm guns, with the LLs not hitting short range until 5 hexes, but the LB2s' minimum starting at 4 hexes. The rockets, too, are more of a nice-to-have than anything you can count on, with the double drawbacks of their penalty to hit and the fickle cluster table determining their damage. Still, hell, I think I'd pay 1,348 BV for this, as long as I've got an objective to park it on.

Lynn's Rating: ...C?

JM6-S

Would you believe we've finally hit the original JagerMech, after all this time? The J. Michael 6 Straczynski is The DD But IntroTech (so, worse). Two AC/2s, two AC/5s, two tons of ammo for the 5s, one ton for the 2s (in the CT, naturally), a medium laser in each side torso, and the thinnest armor a JagerMech ever mounts: 13/16/13 and 3/5/3 pips on the front and rear torsos, six pips on the arms, and 11 on the legs.

It's 901 BV, and that's not nothing, but if you have any access to the DDa, it's an improvement over this in every regard.

Lynn's Rating: D+.

Warrior House Imarra JagerMech. Credit: Lynn B.

The JM7 Series

Before we get into the JM7 JagerMechs, I want to note that they move up to 70 tons, are referred to under the moniker "JagerMech II" in-universe, and yet are officially categorized on the Master Unit List as the same mech as the preceding JagerMechs, while the "JagerMech III," which is 65 tons and shares the JM6 model number, is officially a separate mech.

Sometimes I hate it here.

(Although it is pretty neat that apparently the JM7s exist to canonize the mistakenly-overweight JagerMech from the MechCommander games!)

Anyway...

JM7-C3BS

This Jihad-era variant mounts two Light AC/2s and a Snub-Nose PPC in each arm, an emotional support ER Medium Laser in the CT, and the C3 Boosted Slave which gives it its moniker. With 13 DHS, this is neutral at a run firing the ACs and Snubs, or gains 3+ Movement on an Alpha Strike. The extra tonnage is very kind to the armor coat here; our -C3BS carries 24/34/24 and 6/6/6 pips on the front and rear torsos and 22 on each limb. That's thin on the rear and a little light on the legs, but phenomenal by JagerMech standards.

This mech's 1,354 BV doesn't really want to eat the increased C3 surcharge that the ECM-penetrating Boosted system gets stuck with, but it is very cost effective on its own as a mech that can throw around a pair of ten-pointers at a nine-hex range thanks to those snubbies while also spitting Precision mosquito bites at your opponent's fast-movers and/or spinning to win with four chances each turn to crit their big boys with AP ammo. LAC/2s get so much ammo per ton that even with four guns you will have enough of both types if you take a ton of Precision and a ton of AP, it's great.

I can't lie: I, personally, am feeling very bullish on this mech right now. I'll be taking it to Southern Assault, one of the largest Classic BattleTech tournaments in the country, this weekend, in a list which coalesced around the fact that the Capellans salvage this thing from the Feddies in large enough numbers that it shows up on their availability list. Once again, it's not a world-beater, but at less than 1400 BV it doesn't have to be. It's just a solid budget heavy with good reach, and I like the cut of its jib.

Lynn's Rating: This B may be revised in my tournament report.

JM7-D

The original JM7, this has the same armor and heat sinks as the -C3BS, but for weapons it mounts an ER Large Laser and an Ultra AC/5 in each arm and two MPLs in the CT. That's a touch spicy for its sinking - it builds 2+ Movement heat if both of the Ultras double-tap alongside the ERLLs - but it's manageable. This isn't a bad set of guns or a bad chassis, but it runs you 1500 BV, and I'd rather have the -C3BS even if it wasn't a savings over this.

Lynn's Rating: C.

JM7-DD

This Rec Guide variant is more interesting... By swapping to Endo-Composite Structure (not the kind that takes double damage) and an XL Gyro it finds weight to mount a Clan-grade Ultra AC/10 and a LAC/5 in each arm, a Spheroid ERML in each side torso, and CASE II in each side torso for its four tons of UAC/10 ammo and two tons of LAC/5, while maintaining the usual JM7 armor coverage. Double-Ds here does drop down to 11 DHS, meaning that it builds 2+ Movement heat on an alpha strike, but that's entirely manageable.

This is a phenomenal increase in damage output for the modest price bump to 1,690 BV. The XL Gyro is a weak spot, but CT crits are always a bad time regardless; I feel the CASE II is a bigger gain to survivability than the XL Gyro is a loss.

Shame this one's still FedSuns-exclusive!

Lynn's Rating: B+.

JM7-F

I'm kind of shocked it took us this long to get to the first Rotary Autocannon variant! Franklin here mounts a RAC/5 in each arm, four tons of ammo (all in the CASE-protected left torso), the same CT MPLs as the JM7-D, a Guardian ECM suite, and a Targeting Computer. At a slightly wasteful 12 DHS, it's heat-negative even if it rips off a running Alpha Strike with the RACs at full spin. Armor is still the same as the other JM7s.

I don't like RACs even half as much as Liberty does, but this is a good caddy for them, and 1,774 BV is a reasonable cost with the TarComp factored in. Given that this is another JagerMech my Capellans, ah, borrow, I should take it for a spin sometime!

Lynn's Rating: B?

JM7-G

Leaning back into the whole "anti-aircraft mech" thing, the -G here mounts an LB 2-X and a RAC/2 in each arm with two tons of ammunition for each set of guns (split across both side torsos and CASE'd in each location) alongside an ERML in each side torso. At the same 13 DHS as the -C3BS and the -D, it's neutral on a running alpha strike, and its armor is the same as all the other JM7s.

It's kind of funny how close this comes to the output of the Bane/Kraken for 1,278 BV, but unless I'm actually taking pot-shots at planes, I'd rather pay a little extra BV for a JM7 that can deal damage in larger clusters.

Lynn's Rating: C- is for Cheap-minus.

JagerMech. Credit: Rockfish

The JagerMech III

Practically speaking, the distinguishing features of the JagerMech III relative to JagerMech Classic are that it picks up an endo-steel skeleton to save extra weight and that it puts those weight savings into a larger XL engine which grants it 5/8/0 speed. Bigger changes have been made to mechs without them officially becoming a different chassis, but the JagerMech III also received a visual facelift in its art, so here we are.

JM6-D3

The basic JagerMech III is kind of a weird side-grade of the JM7-C3BS. Its arms carry a PPC and an Ultra AC/2 each, and it also has a medium laser in each side torso for a token minimum-range bite. It builds movement heat firing the arm guns and isn't likely to want to alpha strike. Armor is solid, but not at the high end of JagerMechs: 22/26/22 and 6/7/6 pips across the front and rear of the torso, 16 on each arm, and 20 on each leg. At its 5/8 speed, this comes out to 1,537 BV.

This mech seems decent, if vulnerable to enemies getting under its arm guns (which all have a minimum range of three hexes), but it doesn't excite me. I don't know what to tell you, the vibes are just off.

Lynn's Rating: C, I guess?

JM6-D4

...huh. Okay, I like this one better than the other JagerMech III, but I have to ask... is this really a JagerMech? It forgot all the bullets! This is the only member of the whole extended JagerMech family which has zero ammunition-fed weapons! It feels closer kin to the Catapult K2K than to its own lineage!

Anyway, this one is basically a D3 which trades away the Ultra 2s to pick up a pair of Light PPCs in the arms, an extra pair of Medium Lasers in the CT, four more Double Heat Sinks, and full armor coverage. Yes, I said full, so this carries the distinction of being the ONLY JagerMech which doesn't under-armor the legs relative to the torso! Progress is real, y'all.

This has a good idea with its bracket-fire set-up. It's neutral at a run firing the arm guns, with their 3-hex minimums... where things go a bit askew is when it hits Medium Laser range. It feels like it wants to drop the Light PPCs in favor of all the MLs, only building movement heat while firing the PPCs plus all four MLs and moving from 30 to 40 damage output in the process, but the PPCs also hit minimum range at the MLs' short range. This mech feels like it would've enjoyed Snub PPCs over the regular PPCs, though I'm not entirely sure what it would do with an extra two tons... Angel ECM, maybe? Or it could turn two of the MLs into MPLs, I suppose. As-is, you're still going to fire the PPCs + MLs when you're at close range, and you're just going to have to eat the fact that you'll always be at a slightly suboptimal range for something.

Anyway, the Catapult K2K's PPC range advantage is real, but it's pretty impressive how much more tonnage for Stuff this gains in comparison to that mech through its additional weight-savings tech and more modest heat-sinking, and it's only 115 BV more expensive at 1,831.

Lynn's Rating: B-.

Final Thoughts

Only a few months ago I mocked the JagerMech in conversation for being universally bad and was embarrassed by being shown evidence that it actually has several decent variants. Many, perhaps even most, JagerMechs are more properly in The Gargoyle Prime Zone: woefully unsuited for a duel with a peer-by-tonnage, but BV-efficient and possessed of real utility when considered on that merit. Some of its variants do spec it in more "conventionally optimal" directions, like the JM6-D4 and the JM7-DD, and that's fine. Where the JagerMech goes wrong is when it takes one of the bargain-basement iterations of its chassis and then straps real guns to it, making it a priority target, like the DG and DGr do. It just needs to pick a lane and stick with it.

Til next time, MechWarriors, remember that building walls to contain extradimensional kaiju is a temporary solution!

title: Our new, Highly Unofficial Warhammer 40k Detachment lets any Space Marine chapter ride monstrous cavalry
content:
Warhammer 40k might focus on the big name Space Marine chapters, but part of the fun of the setting has always been creating your own custom army with distinctive paint scheme, backstory, and miniature conversions. We've put together a free 40k detachment that allows any Space Marine chapter to field mounted marines riding monstrous cavalry, to encourage more awesome conversions.

Beastrider Cavalry is a free, unofficial Space Marine detachment. It costs one Detachment Point and its Force Disposition is Reconnaissance. As this is a fanmade detachment you'll need your opponent's permission to use it - so if you think anything is unbalanced with it, make like a Techmarine and adjust it. Let us know in the Wargamer Discord community what changes you made and why!

You can download the detachment as a PDF here.

I was inspired to make this detachment by some excellent Howling Griffons demigryph-riders, and there are a lot of great monster mounts that will work as the basis for conversions - Stormcast Eternals mounts, the Kroot Lone Spear's Kalamandras, even weirder creatures like the Sylvaneth Spiteriders or Idoneth Allopex could work.

To keep the rules simple, the units use the unaltered stats for Thunderwolf Cavalry. A choice of four enhancements (all of them Upgrades) then allow you to better tailor them to reflect your conversions.

  • Predatory Haste - re-roll advance rolls.
  • Stealth Predators - gain Scouts 12″.
  • Living Bulwark - attacks that target the unit have -1D.
  • Relentless - gain Mobile.

The three Stratagems are inspired by those available to the Thunderwolves in various detachments; one to give them some extra damage on the charge, then two out-of-turn movement tricks, one to lock enemies into melee, the other to reposition away from shooting.

  • Linebreaking Charge - inflict mortal wounds after charging.
  • Relentless Pursuit - a D3+3″ surge move after an enemy unit falls back from engagement.
  • Calculated Withdrawal - a D3+3″ reactive move after an enemy unit shoots.

If you test this detachment out and have feedback, or have an idea for a narrative detachment you'd really like to see, let us know in the Wargamer Discord community. We're slowly developing a little library of Highly Unofficial detachments:

  • Angels Among Us - lone Space Marines bolstering humble Astra Militarum
  • Looted Motorpool - Ork looted vehicles.

title: Games from the Crypt #25 - So Say We All!
content:
Games maker Ghost Galaxy has just announced an absolute shocker of a reprint, one that I thought would absolutely never happen. It's a game that has been out of print now for many years, largely due to rights issues, which has been a travesty because it is also the best and most important game released in the 21st century. Like Dune before it, itself the best and most important game of its decade, it is has languished in unavailability. And also like Dune, a quite terrible rethemed reprint of it popped up a couple of years ago that seemed to ignore the fact that the original setting, characters, and concepts were part of what made it great. Aftermarket copies have been well into eye-watering levels for years at this point, making me regret selling the game at what was already "guitar money" for me several years back.

Of course this game being exhumed from the Games Crypt is none other than Corey Koniezcka's masterpiece and the best original design that Fantasy Flight Games ever published - 2008's Battlestar Galactica. The game is to be produced with the full Universal-licensed livery and with former FFG and current Ghost Galaxy honcho Christian Petersen overseeing affairs. Sadly, it is going to be a crowdfunded product which diminishes my enthusiasm considerably, but at least the game will most likely be treated with dignity and respect it deserves.

Back when it released, it hit like a nuke across the bow of a Basestar. The show was hot, with another season left to go, and it was something that my entire friend group and gaming community were definitely very much into. At that point, FFG had built up a considerable reputation for high quality, well-designed narrative adventure games so it was a big release all around despite Mr. Koniezcka being a relatively unknown designer at the time. It was also coming a few years on from previous semi co-op hidden traitor games like Shadows Over Camelot, which had been very successful. And it was lightning in a bottle.

I recall the first plays- it felt fresh, exciting, and new mechanically with compelling and very tangible themes around suspicion, paranoia, distrust, survivalism, and sacrifice. These were all the themes of the show, and players got to take on the roles of characters like Bill Adama, Kara Thrace, and Gaius Baltar. The trials and tribulations of the ship were writ large in the game, with everything from personal drama to logistical catastrophes to seat-of-the-pants space battles represented. And just like the show, the twist is that one - or two - of the players are secretly Cylons infiltrating the Galactica and working at cross purposes.

The mechanism was absolutely brilliant. Crises would occur, and players contributed cards to help resolve them. But the Cylon player was called upon to use there cards to sabotage efforts and to do so in a way that would keep other players from figuring out their identity. This meant lying about the "best card" you could play that actually tanked the entire ship, or obfuscating bad behavior with counter-accusations. It was an intensely social game that emphasized soft skills like conversation, observation, and intuition rather than the usual board game value assessments and comprehension of board state related to mechanics.

When you were discovered, you'd get airlocked. So the best thing to do would be to get innocent characters airlocked instead of you. Shrewd Cylon players could be tough to beat, and the big reveal was never less than shocking and dramatic. Jokes are still made in many groups today about who is or is not the Cylon. It is the post-millennium "wood for sheep".

My group played BSG for years after it came out, and it had longevity I had not seen since Settlers of Catan in the late 90s. It was never less than great. It was always requested, and expansions helped to keep it fresh by bringing in elements from the last seasons such as Admiral Cain and the Battlestar Pegasus. I felt like the expansions sort of over-extended the game and over-complicated some things, but I still bought them, played them, and enjoyed them. It is unclear as to whether the Ghost Galaxy edition will reprint them or include some or all of their content in the package.

The genius of the game - again, like Dune - is that it so perfectly used gameplay mechanics and subject matter to get players to act and make decisions like the characters from the source material. The big concepts and themes are described and players interact directly with and through them as well as with each other as these are highly engaged games that are definitely not for those who prefer heads-down contemplation of individual player boards. The thrill is in participating in arguments, discussions, and debates all framed by mechanics that provide structure but never get in the way with clutter, cruft, or empty processes.

Few games reach this level of absolute genius, and it was surprising at the time to see a licensed game do exactly that. I had for years prior said that you knew a game was going to suck when it had still images from a show or movie on the components. This upended that rhetoric, and it set a spectacularly high standard for licensed titles that I think is still the bar today.

title: D&D World of Warcraft classes: winners and losers
content:
The D&D World of Warcraft book is a momentous crossover. It's D&D's first Universes Beyond product, the first of many supplements that explores pop culture's most beloved IPs. Whether you love or loathe the concept, one thing can't be denied - our DnD classes are getting a heap of new rules to play with.

We're not just talking about subclasses here, either. Some core classes have been completely reflavored, with new replacement abilities as well as a host of new subclasses. At the same time, many of fifth edition's favorite subclasses appear here as reprints. It's a mish-mash of content, some old and some new.

I've been through the new book with a fine-toothed comb, prepping theory builds and pondering rules interactions. Based on this read-through review, here are the classes I think fared best and worst:

Winner: Barbarian

Barbarians have been re-tooled to represent World of Warcraft Shamans. I have very limited WoW experience, but many MMO veterans have (rather loudly) pointed out how poorly this shoe fits. Barbarians aren't equipped to represent the magical capabilities of Shamans, so this feels like a thematic mismatch.

Mechanically, though, there's far more good than bad. The base Barbarian's Primal Knowledge is replaced by Totems, which you can plant in the ground as a bonus action to create a 30-foot emanation. Your totem might decrease enemy speed, increase ally speed, give immunity to charmed and frightened, or simply give all your pals access to Primal Knowledge.

It's a nice perk if you're expecting to defend a specific patch of ground, but generally, it's a tactically terrible idea for characters to cluster together and not move. Overall, Totems are so-so.

Onto subclasses. The Barbarian gets two in this book, the reprinted Path of the Spiritual Guardian and the all-new Path of the Elements.

You might remember the first under its former name, Path of the Ancestral Guardian. This was a defense-focused Barbarian that, while it didn't quite match most players' one-man-killing-machine fantasy, was incredibly strong regardless.

It's still both of those things, as very little has changed for this reprint. Spiritual Protectors now lets you choose to deal extra damage or use the Slow weapon mastery alongside another option - though you can still give foes disadvantage when attacking everyone except you. Spirit Shield now scales with your Rage damage bonus, which makes minimal difference to the damage it reduces. Consult the Spirits is identical, though your capstone is completely different (and, in my opinion, too situational to get really excited about). Now, you get to perform an extra attack if you roll 18 to 20 on your D20.

I don't expect Path of the Elements to run away with the Barbarian build meta, but it's pretty damn effective. At level three, Raging Elements allows you to make an elemental attack as part of your Rage action, or as a bonus action on future turns while raging. Its three options deal a few dice of elemental damage on a hit, and they set up the next attack of a different damage type to roll additional dice. There's some neat strategizing to be done here, even though it's tempting to spam Icefury, the option that deals the most damage.

Level six lets you cast Elementalism, Daylight, Water Walk, or Wind Wall as Wisdom spells - and that's fine, just fine. Level 10's resistance to cold, fire, and lightning damage also feels a little 'meh' for its level tier, but the capstone ups the excitement again. Elemental Overload modifies your Raging Elements features so that, whether they hit or miss, they debuff or damage your foe in some way. That's a pretty tantalizing freebie, and you've still got your main action for axe-swinging.

Loser: Bard

There is no Bard in World of Warcraft. Sorry, songstrels!

Winner: Cleric

Clerics stand in for World of Warcraft's Priests, with two new subclasses to represent the latter's love of Light or Void. Both the Discipline Cleric and the Shadow Cleric have their clunky moments, but at least one of them is well worth playing. Plus, as our guide to WoW's best spells show, the Cleric spell list gets some very exciting new toys.

Discipline Clerics balance offense and defense with a strong spell list and the Holy Bolt feature, a bonus action attack that deals radiant damage while simultaneously healing a creature within 60 feet. It costs a use of your Channel Divinity, but otherwise it's more cost-effective than spamming Healing Word.

Also at level three come Atonement, Discipline's signature ability. When you heal someone with a leveled spell, you bless them until the end of your next turn. If you deal damage with a leveled spell in that time, your blessed buds gain extra HP. Fiddly to set up consistently, but pretty neat!

Atonement is more worth the hassle after level six. From here on, you can use a bonus action and Channel Divinity to give blessed allies Temporary HP. As long as they have temporary HP, your friends are resistant to all damage.

Then, you get nothing until level 17, when your Holy Bolt gives you the power to teleport 30 feet before an attack, or spend a spell slot to fire off additional bolts. This Cleric's tactics take a lot of planning, but it seems like a solid all-rounder subclass.

Shadow Clerics seem less explosive. The domain spells are B-grade, with a few choice cuts like Evard's Black Tentacles. Level three gives you a bonus action Shadow Form that lets you hide in dim light or darkness, or deal extra damage after a spell doles out psychic or necrotic damage. Both situational, and both profoundly 'alright'. The same goes for Devouring Plague, a level-three ability that deals extra necrotic damage to a target you see fail a saving throw.

Things get better with level six, where you can spend a reaction to become shadowy energy after taking a hit. You have 40 feet of fly speed and resistance to all damage in this form, and you can't take any kind of action until the end of your next turn. During that time, you can spend Hit Point Dice to recover health.

Lastly, there's level 17's Vampiric Embrace. While your Shadow Form is active, you heal a target whenever you roll extra damage. It's a situational capstone for a subclass that, apart from its level-six failsafe, doesn't have much unique to offer.

Loser: Druid

D&D's most neglected subclass goes another book without any new subclasses. Wizards makes up for it by giving us some fantastic new spells - Wrath, Moonfire, Starfall, and Innervate, among others. But, if you're a diehard Druid player, that's not nearly enough value to justify buying a whole book.

Loser: Fighter

Fighters have been reskinned as Warriors for World of Warcraft. That brings no new subclasses, but it does offer a few additional maneuvers to Battle Masters. They're all decent, but I don't expect many to oust the current optimal options.

Battle Shout gives allies within 30 feet who hear your cry the power to add your Superiority Die to a damage roll the next time it attacks. Meanwhile, Demoralizing Shout subtracts your Superiority Die from the next damage roll made by enemies within 30 feet.

Heroic Leap lets you jump feet equal to your Strength score, forcing a Strength save and potential bludgeoning damage on creatures within five feet of where you land. It's a nice bit of movement and extra damage, even offering half damage on a successful save.

Next, Mortal Strike prevents a creature you just hit with an attack roll from healing. Your Superiority Die is added to the damage roll, and the target can't heal until the end of your next turn.

Last comes Warding Maneuver, a reaction that triggers when you or an adjacent ally is hit by an attack roll - but only if you're wielding a melee weapon or shield. Meet those conditions, and you add your Superiority Die's result to the target's AC. Plus, if the attack still hits, the target is resistant to its damage.

Some of these are pretty neat! But it's very little added value when compared with other classes.

Winner: Monk

Monks keep their name and disciplines, with the only new content being a single subclass and a handful of feats. That subclass is Warrior of Mystic Brews, formerly known as the Way of the Drunken Warrior. This tipsy Monk looks basically identical to its old form in the early levels, but it's unrecognizable by tier two.

The biggest change comes with level six's Mystic Brew, which uses Brewer's Supplies to craft magical beverages. Cinnamon Dragon lets you exhale a 30-foot cone of flame that also poisons the unlucky target. Heavenly Spirit offers two damage resistances, while Refreshing Dip makes healing yourself more effective. These benefits last an hour, but spending a Focus Point extends the effects to eight hours.

You learn more brews at level 11, unlocking the power to add Unarmed Strikes to reactions, gain Heroic Inspiration, or double up on Patient Defense. Then, your capstone allows one brew to offer two effects. Level 17 also gets a second bonus capstone that lets you spam unarmed strikes while moving with Patient Defense.

It's a significant upgrade to a subclass that was fun but not overly impressive. The new feats, designed for but not exclusive to Monks, aren't too shabby either. One lets you Dodge as a reaction after taking damage, while another reaction wraps an ally in a cocoon that absorbs incoming damage.

The third treats any 1 on an unarmed strike or Light weapon attack's damage die as a two, and adds a +1 bonus to unarmed strike attacks for every time you've hit previously on the same turn. Lastly, we have a feat that reduces delays by creating a Delayed Reaction pool, which is rolled at the end of your turn to determine the damage you actually take. All of these can be taken from level four, and they offer some really interesting Monk synergies.

Winner: Paladin

The Paladin gets two separate sections in the classes chapter. First comes the Death Knight, a distinct 'Hero Class' that starts life at level three. Basically, this is a special subclass - known as the Oath of the Ebon Blade - that replaces some of a regular Paladin's features. And, honestly, it looks sick as all hell.

Death Knight

Lay on Hands is usurped by Death Coil, which gives you a pool of D8s and a new bonus action that forces a creature within 60 feet to make a Con save. If it fails, it takes necrotic damage equal to a roll of your D8s. Alternatively, if the target is Undead, it regains that many HP.

The subclass' spell list doesn't excite much, but Runeforging does. This level-three feature lets you inscribe a rune on your weapon during a long rest. The Blood rune gives you temporary HP equal to your Charisma modifier and Paladin level, both when you inscribe the rune or kill an enemy with your weapon. The Frost rune means your weapon ignores cold damage resistance, and you deal 1d4 extra cold damage when you make a Light weapon's extra attack. Lastly, the Unholy rune ignores necrotic damage resistance, and it deals extra necrotic damage (equal to your Charisma modifier) if you're attacking with a Heavy weapon.

Paladin's Smite is replaced by Runic Smite, a new smiting spell that deals necrotic damage. From level three, you can also spend a use of Channel Divinity after you cast the smite. Depending on your chosen Rune, you can regain HP, deal extra cold damage, or subtract 1D6 from the target's next saving throw.

At higher tiers, Paladin's get a modified Faithful Steed with a new bonus action that lets the steed and its rider move through solid objects. Their Aura of Protection grants resistance to cold, necrotic, and psychic damage, and at level 11, Radiant Strikes becomes Runic Strikes - a feature that adds 1d8 necrotic damage to melee attack rolls.

But wait, there's more! Instead of Restoring Touch, you get Improved Death Coil, which adds extra necrotic damage or healing to Death Coil, regardless of whether your target failed its saving throw.

Level 15 upgrades your runes with a new once-per-long-rest ability, offering damage-reducing reactions, a 30-foot cone AoE attack, or the power to cast a version of Summon Undead that lasts one minute without concentration.

Finally, we have a capstone bonus action. For 10 minutes, you can spend a level-four spell slot to recover a Runic Mastery use, and you can choose any effect from Runic Power or Runic Mastery, not just the one specific to your currently carved rune.

The Death Knight feels as fun as it does flavorful. But that's not the only new Paladin on the block…

Oath of the Holy

This new subclass is available to all kinds of Paladin players, and it's a pretty fantastic healer. Cure Wounds, Healing Word, Lesser Restoration, Death Ward, and more all feature on the spell list. You can spend Channel Divinity to wrap an ally in holy light for a minute, so when you heal any other target, that creature regains half as many HP.

From level seven, Lightbringer's Aura adds 1D6 to your Lay on Hands if you target a Bloodied creature in your Aura of Protection. Then, from level 15, you refresh your Lay on Hands pool any time you cast a spell that deals radiant damage, with the points regained equal to the radiant damage rolled.

Finally, our level-20 capstone is a bonus action that gives your Aura of Protection additional benefits for 10 minutes. When a Bloodied ally starts its turn within the aura, it automatically regains HP equal to your Charisma modifier and proficiency bonus. Plus, the aura is filled with bright sunlight.

Is it a better healer than a Life Cleric? Maybe not, but it allows the Paladin to juggle the Healer role alongside its other responsibilities effortlessly.

Winner: Ranger

Like the Paladin, the Ranger gets a regular class update and a 'heroic class' with its own distinct identity. There's also an optional new Pet Specialization rule for the Beast Master subclass (which makes you and your Primal Companion much stronger), but the main dish here is the new Demon Hunter.

Demon Hunters are just like regular Rangers at first, only they get a Fighting Style at level two. You can choose any you like, the Druidic Warrior option from the Player's Handbook, or an all-new Void Warrior option that teaches you two Warlock cantrips.

Demon Hunters have a dedicated spell list from level three, and there are some explosive options here. You'll be familiar with Misty Step, Banishment, and Steel Wind Strike already. Less familiar are the new spells in this book - and many of the best picks are exclusive to the Demon Hunter. Seriously, Throw Glaive, Chaos Nova, Fel Rush, Eye Beam, and Demon Spikes are all worth your attention.

Demon Hunters have 10 feet of blindsight at level three, as well as the Soul Fragments feature. This is a pool of tiny objects equal to your Wisdom modifier that appears at the start of each day, and you can spend them on various effects.

At first, you've only got Double Jump - a free cast of Feather Fall or Jump - and Soul Cleave. That second one lets you replace one of your attacks with a 10-foot AoE attack that deals 1D12 + your Wisdom modifier in psychic damage on a failed Dex save. You also regain HP equal to your Wisdom modifier as an added bonus.

Level seven gives creatures affected by Hunter's Mark disadvantage on attacks against everyone except you. Plus, once per turn when you hit that creature, you can subtract 1D4 from its next saving throw or deal an extra 1D8 Fire damage. Hunter's Mark is still a divisive part of the 5.5e Ranger's design, but it's not going anywhere, so these buffs are very welcome.

At level 11, you get two new ways to spend Soul Fragments. Two of them lets you cast Counterspell, or you can spend one to cast Throw Glaive (one of the best new spells in your arsenal) for free. Then, at level 15, Soul Cleave improves, offering 2D12 + Wisdom modifier damage. Oh, and you regain a soul fragment on rolling Initiative if you have none.

Lastly, at level 18, the Demon Hunter replaces the Ranger's Feral Senses feature with 30 feet of blindsight. This is a Ranger that doesn't have a flashy gimmick, but it's an exceptionally good defender backed up by simple yet strong spellcasting options.

Winner: Rogue

WoW Rogues get just one subclass reprint, but what a reprint it is. The Swashbuckler returns for 5.5e, and it's still a solid subclass option, safe yet satisfying to play. Your early features, Fancy Footwork and Rakish Audacity, are reprinted as-is, but Wizards has made more significant changes in later levels.

Case in point: Panache at level nine. This now gives you two new ways to use Cunning Strike. Spend 1D6 Sneak Attack dice, you force your target to make a Wisdom save or have disadvantage on attack rolls against anyone but you. You're also the only one they can target with opportunity attacks. Alternatively, spend 3D6, and creatures within 30 feet are Charmed for a turn unless they pass a Wisdom save.

At level 13, Dashing Strikes adds two new Cunning Strike options. Spend 2D6, and you allow a creature to add 1D6 to attack rolls and saving throws until the end of their next turn. Alternatively, also for 2D6, you roll a D6 and add it to your AC until the start of your next turn.

Lastly, at level 17, you can make a second attack against a target after using your Sneak Attack, provided no other creatures are within five feet. None of the Swashbuckler's new powers are potent to the point of broken, but they feel suitably snazzy for one of my favorite Rogue subclasses.

Loser: Sorcerer

The Sorcerer has been reflavored as a WoW Evoker, but no new subclasses aid this transition. We get several new Sorcerer spells, and some of them are pretty sweet, offering new ways to heal, deal damage, or debuff foes (usually by reducing their speed). The new spells help Sorcerers specialize in party roles they might not otherwise touch, but none of the book's best spells appear in this list. That means Sorcerer players have even less to get excited about than Druid lovers.

Loser: Warlock

There's no subclasses for the World of Warcraft Warlock, and they only get three new spells to play with. Admittedly, those spells look like fun. Curse of Agony forces a target to keep making Con saves until they fail - and every time they succeed, the damage die gets bigger and more painful. Hand of Gul'dan chucks a demonic meteor, dealing necrotic and fire damage in a 20-foot sphere. And Rain of Fire is a huge cylinder of fire you can move around to deal damage - and gain advantage on attacks against those inside.

Beyond this, all we get are new Eldritch Invocations. That sounds exciting at first, but then you realize Wizards has given us a slightly worse version of Pact of the Chain. Instead of an Imp, you can summon a Fel Imp, which does similar amounts of damage, but doesn't have any of the same utility. You can summon alternate creatures (especially if you take Legion Summoning at level nine), but there's not much here that feels new and shiny.

Plus, the non-Pact Invocations feel a little bland. Curse of Corruption deals a small dose of extra necrotic damage to cursed targets at the start of their turn. Expendable Minions heals you or a friend when a familiar you control dies, and Health Funnel lets you spend Hit Dice to keep a familiar alive. Last, we have Master Demonologist, that lets fiends under your command benefit from Hex's extra damage. I can't see many of these usurping the current Invocations of choice from the Player's Handbook.

Loser: Wizard

Another class that's been reduced to build suggestions and a handful of new spells is the Wizard, now referred to as the Mage. You get four spells to play with, and while the Wizard hardly needs more overpowered options, it's still a bit of a lackluster list. Flurry, a single-target cold damage attack that restrains, is one of the better ones, as is Combustion, an ongoing AoE of fire damage that also gives you advantage on spell attack rolls.

Beyond this, we get three new feats intended for a Mage/Wizard, and only one is really worth talking about. Hot Streak lets you ignore resistance to fire damage, and when your spell deals fire damage to a creature, they start burning. If they're already burning, the burning damage increases by 1d4. Basically, this gives your Fireballs more bang for their buck. Spicy!

That's all on World of Warcraft for now, but our full review is on the way. If you want to check it out, join our Wargamer Discord to be the first to hear about all future D&D coverage.

title: Tabletop Battles Reviews: Queen's Domain
content:
Saying that Dark Souls casts a long shadow over the entire action-RPG subgenre is somehow both a completely true statement while also wildly underselling it. The game has become a cultural phenomenon since its 2011 release, and the staggering popularity of Dark Souls has spawned a new wave of interest and homage to its spiritual predecessor, the first-person dungeon crawler King’s Field. In the last few years, games like Lunacid, Dread Delusion, and Labyrinth of the Demon king have put their own spin on the King’s Field formula, riding high on the popularity of “retro” style indie releases that aim to emulate the look and feel of late-PlayStation era games.

This new wave of dungeon crawlers, or “field-like” games, all face the same problem. In a subgenre designed specifically to emulate another game, how do you step out of the shadow of King’s Field? How do you go from being simply a love letter to something that stands tall on its own merit, especially now that this renaissance of retro dungeon crawlers becomes crowded with new titles?

Rather than trying to stand out by subverting the genre and adding some new twist to the gameplay formula, Queen’s Domain instead takes the legacy of King’s Field head on, to the point where even the name Queen’s Domain is an unsubtle play on words. For the small team at Freshly Baked Games, success lied in both fully embracing what made the King’s Field games a cult classic before Dark Souls put From Software on the map, while also innovating and evolving on the dungeon crawler formula in ways that feel decidedly modern.

In other words, Queen’s Domain’s plan to escape the shadow of King’s Field is to simply make a better King’s Field. Not only does the game succeed, Queen’s Domain knocks it out of the park.

Credit: Freshly Baked Games

Stranger in a Strange Land

Fittingly for its retro gaming stylings, Queen’s Domain is light on story, with the only sizable chunk of direct storytelling happening in the game’s intro cutscene. It's a pretty generic fantasy adventure setup, the evil Queen has returned from beyond the grave and is gathering an army of evil on the mysterious island of Neasied. The King sent out an expedition to stop her, but hasn’t been heard from in some time. You play as Prince Berium, who is leading a second expedition to find out what happened to the King and, if needed, finish the job he started.  As you approach the island however, the Queen summons a terrible storm that claims your ship and scatters your crew.

After that, the game kicks off proper as you awake on the shores of Neasied, without a weapon or plan to speak of, and take your first look around the island. Queen’s Domain’s environments are fantastically realized, and range from some traditional mysterious ruins and near pitch-black dungeons, to stranger stuff like esoteric arcane forests and a few late game areas that are a complete left-turn. While all of these areas are unique visually from one another, the one thing that they all have in common is that they’re all dripping with atmosphere.

Credit: Freshly Baked Games

Queen’s Domain nails the feeling of mystery and dread that comes with exploring Neasied by often using the limitations of the PlayStation era graphics to its advantage. The lower resolution obscures details and intensifies the darkness, and it’s often difficult to discern details from a long distance. True old school gaming sickos can even stick with the default “retro” filter applied to closer represent the resolution found on older screens, but personally I found this setting to muddy the visuals a bit too much, and considering how well executed those environments are I wanted to ensure I was getting a clear look at them.

The strong visual atmosphere is coupled with a fantastic sound design. Queen’s Domain is a quiet game, its soundscape never really becomes bombastic, but it's never quiet. There's always the sound of something, like your own footsteps or shuffling lizards, alongside the groans and hisses of monsters as they wander the world. The whole effect works best with headphones, since you often hear enemies before you see them you’ll keep a sharp ear for any sound that's out of place. A few times I was even stopped cold in my tracks, ready for a fight, only to discover the noise was just a rat scuttling underfoot.

I also nearly leapt six feet from my chair the first time I heard the truly awful screeching sound of this game’s treasure lizards, so Queen’s Domain knows when to get loud too.

The synth-heavy ambient soundtrack keeps to the background during the games runtime, rarely ever asserting itself to really dominate the scene, but acting as a real workhorse to bring the whole mood together. Earlier areas in the island sun tend to be more mysterious in tone, while the sounds for later underground bits elevate the danger by upping the tempo. It’s hard to say that there’s any standout tracks here, aside from song that plays when you go to the shop that heavily features duck quacks, but every single music piece for each area accentuates the mood and improves immersion.

Credit: Freshly Baked Games

Flash of the Blade

After washing up the beach and wandering up the shore a bit, you run into a few of your companions from the boat who provide you a weapon, a rusty blade, and point you in the direction of the king, who went through some big tomb doors that they haven’t any idea how to enter. Their company is short-lived, and by the time I broke down the nearby barrier to unlock my first saving crystal, the knights had mysteriously died. With rusty sword in hand, it was time to confront whatever monsters awaited for me on this bizarre island.

Combat in Queen's Domain at the most basic level is basically the exact same as it was in King’s Field, though very early on the game provides you with some extra tools that add some fun twists to the formula. At its core, combat is much more deliberate than most modern games and centers around your stamina bar, which empties with every attack before refilling. Each attack with your weapon is a commitment, and like its spiritual predecessor, attacks only do appreciable damage when the stamina bar is full. Spamming attacks with an empty bar will only succeed in tickling a monster. For maximum damage, attacks can be held and charged as well. Since there is no dodge roll or block to speak of, managing your space by constantly moving and baiting out attacks before punishing them is key.

Credit: Freshly Baked Games

It's a glacial system by modern standards, but Queen’s Domain does have a few tricks up its sleeve to make the combat more engaging. Each one of the over fifty weapons has a secondary attack alongside their primary attack, which can range from a lunging strike in the case of the starting sword to a magical attack that charges up as you deal damage. You quickly find a magical dagger belt fairly early on as well, which gives you access to ranged attacks. Ranged weapon option includes a variety of throwing daggers, chakrams, and darts that have a limited number of uses but don’t cost stamina, instead slowly recharging over time, making them great for pulling enemies away from groups or keeping up damage while your stamina refills. Each weapon also has a damage type, and every enemy has resistances and weakness to a certain types of damage, making weapon swapping between one of your three equipped weapons key in any given fight.

Even with all of these tools, rushing headlong into fights is a pretty bad idea. Healing items don’t replenish, and dying doesn’t send you back to a checkpoint but is instead a hard game over, forcing you to reload your last save at one of the aforementioned saving crystals. These are plentiful around the island, but they're also the only place you can save, so an unexpected death can wipe a big chunk of progress.

Combine all of this together, and it creates a combat loop that feels less like an Elder Scrolls game and more like a survival horror title. You need to mind your space and make sure you’re using the right tool for the job, all while ensuring you do everything you can to avoid getting hit and draining your precious supply of healing items. It makes combat against multiple enemies a delightfully tense affair, as you’re constantly switching between your weapons and toolset while kiting along the monsters that pursue you. Especially with the huge roster of weapons and monsters with different moves and abilities, including some truly out there ones later on in the game, combat remains tense and engaging throughout the whole game.

Credit: Freshly Baked Games

The Magic of Discovery

The combat is good, probably the most solid system out of any of the new wave of Field-like games, but where Queen’s Domain truly sings is in its exploration, which rewards experimentation and curiosity like very few titles do. Queen’s Domain is filled to nearly bursting with puzzles and secrets, and rarely uses any part of it’s map as set dressing. Neasied itself feels like the best combination possible of a great Metroidvania game for its upgrade hunting and secrets and the original Dark Souls with its interconnected map and player freedom. There truly is something remarkable around nearly every turn.

Exploration is good at the start, but it blows wide open when you acquire the Holy Sword Endu after the first boss. Endu has an air dash ability that can be used no matter what weapon you have equipped, and can be upgraded with wind gems to gain access to additional dashes. Suddenly, multiple places on the map that were inaccessible before open up, and every gap becomes a question of “wait, can I make that?” I found myself not only trying to make jumps and cross gaps that felt impossible in other titles, but almost every single time was rewarded for doing so with an item, chest, or upgrade. And your suite of tools for exploration only gets larger as the game goes on, encouraging the player to double back on old zones to grab items they could only glimpse the first time around. Impressively, I never felt frustrated when I backtracked to grab these upgrades. Usually, I was rushing back with barely contained excitement, eager to test if what I’d just discovered is exactly what I’m missing to grab that item, solve that puzzle, or open that chest I couldn’t before.

An early example of this came when I explored an area I’d previously been through before to farm some healing items, when I noticed a ramp I hadn’t before. Climbing up, I saw that hey, the elevation is about level with a platform on the other side of the clearing, which I couldn’t figure out how to reach before. It looked like a pretty decent gap, but with the third air dash I’d just unlocked, it was suddenly very doable, leading to a short climb up to a statue I had seen a few times before that I couldn’t interact with. After seeing several of these things, I decided the must be important, but there wasn’t a clear answer on how to interact with them. After trying a few different things, I found that my magical torch lit the statue’s ablaze, and I nearly jumped out of my seat when I remembered I’d seen a door earlier in my adventure that said I needed to light three statues to pass through. It’s one of dozens of examples of amazing discovery throughout the playthrough, and it made every moment of exploring this strange island a delight.

Credit: Freshly Baked Games

All Hail the Queen

Queen’s Domain isn’t just a solid homage to the King’s Field series that came before it, this game takes the lessons to its predecessor and expands and innovates on them in nearly every single way into a game that feels modern, refreshing, and exciting while remaining wonderfully retro. It deserves to be considered on every single one of its own merits, and it's an absolute triumph of a game. I haven’t felt this sort of wonder and immersion while exploring a game world since Elden Ring, and its hard to overstate how impressive it is that this game, which was made by a team of just two people, has a world that stands toe to toe with one of the most critically acclaimed games of the decade. Queen’s Domain isn’t just my game of the year, it’s one of my favorite games that I’ve played in multiple years. Whether you’re a fan of the King’s Field series that inspired it or just someone who loves a grand video game adventure, I highly recommend playing Queen’s Domain, which feels destined to go down as a gaming classic.

Have any questions or feedback? Drop us a note in the comments below or email us at contact@goonhammer.com. Want articles like this linked in your inbox every Monday morning? Sign up for our newsletter. And don’t forget that you can support us on Patreon for backer rewards like early video content, Administratum access, an ad-free experience on our website and more.

title: Competitive Innovations in 11th: From Talavera to Tokyo
content:
Welcome to Competitive Innovations, our weekly feature for a number of game lines across the tabletop wargame space. Each week our army list and tactics experts canvass the top tournaments for their game of specialty, looking at the week’s top match-ups and how they played out on the tabletop to let you know what’s hot, what’s not, and what might be coming next as the competitive meta evolves year-round.

I...didn't think this could happen any more.

Somehow, we've hit a mystery gap in the event schedule across most of the world, with but a single GT+ singles event, logged from Australia. The UK is, perhaps, recovering from the Coventry UKTC double header. The US had the midterms yesterday, so I assume booking venues for the weekend would have been prohibitively expensive, because politicians needed those for rallies and/or baffling crashouts.

In Europe, it's a slightly different story - lots of players were gathered at the massive Talavera team tournament, which normally we'd have to um and ah about finding space for, but due to the extremely light schedule of regular events, we can happily give some proper attention. Finally, GW ran an official super RTT at the Tokyo Warhammer cafe, so we'll bring that in too. That gives us something that looks enough like a column to be getting on with. For Friday, we'll put together some sort of editorial.

Everyone happy? Let's go.

Thoughts

New Custodes make their first foray into a Showdown, facing off against a daunting challenge from Dark Angels, who are one of the most powerful forces in the current metagame.

On the Custodes side, we have what is quickly emerging as the One True Custodes shell, at least with the points as they stand. The consensus is that those points are a bit high (certainly on the non-Dreadnought units), so you need to build a list that 1. has Dreadnoughts, and 2. squeezes maximum value out of every other model it puts on the table. 2x Allarus squads, Dreadnoughts and support as Lions/Moritoi and your choice of Solar Watch/Emperor's Chosen/Dread Host is the consensus route to achieving that. Lions provides your Terminator squads with high mobility, and allows the second unit to pivot to scoring duties in an emergency via Unleash the Lions. It also provides some defences against highly mobile high threat armies, as Vigil Unending can blunt a key charge, witha  devastating counterattack following. Allarus are also great all-purpose killers thanks to +1 to W against anything they're not already going to mince into a fine paste.

Those are supported by Dreadnoughts, which are just plain good. The Galatus is a phenomenal profile into the current metagame, and the Memento one is a particular nightmare, while a Telemon with a Feel No Pain is good as ever, especially because of how good the overwatch from dual fist flamers is. Finally, a Caladius provides some ranged anti-tank, and is especially strong in variants running Emperor's chosen as here.

What are they up against? Dark Angels. Riding around on their bikes, playing ominous music, and generally making a nuisance of themselves. Vengeances are definitely not what the Custodes want to see, as they are pretty much perfect for chewing through Allarus (and can at least threaten everything else), while the spike damage of the big melee threats also isn't ideal (but a bit dicier thanks to aforementioned Vigil Undending being able to throw off the maths).

I think this is a tough game for the Custodes but not unwinnable - they have more good threats than the Dark Angels can kill fast, and the mission suits them - skulking 12OC of Trajann and Allarus toed next to a ruin on the near side of the central objective forces the Dark Angels to commit pretty hard to shift it, and if that goes even a little bit wrong, things could go very rapidly south for them. They're also distinctly short on things that reliably kill the Telemon - just one Eradipulsor is extremely in the range that can bounce off invulns and just not really do anything.

I think the Dark Angels have to cede the centre for one turn and try and soften the Custodes up a bit, and then go for a big dunk on turn 2 or 3, aiming to close the game out. It helps how good the incidental shooting on the bikes is at clearing out stuff like Sisters of Silence, which can happen during the go turn as almost an afterthought. Legitimately, things could still go either way at that point, and it seems plausible the game could swing hard one way or the other. It would appear that for now, the Unforgiven remain unmoved.

Archetype

Pressure Aeldari

Thoughts

Undefeated elves! Love that for us.

This list is also fully sick, going for proper lightning fast aggression thanks to the speed provided by Eldritch Raiders, and packing in a bunch of units that hit really well into the current metagame. Small squads of Shining Spears and Banshees are both in target-rich environments right now, and with this many units flitting around it's tough for opponents to avoid providing favourable trades. Having access to Jain Zar's unit also provides a bit of a sliding scale of commitment. When you need something really heavy dealt with, both the big Exodite squad and Yriel's unit provide options. The Exodites give you lots of D3 outut (especially if teed up by Lhykhis), which provides more of a deterrant to enemy deathbricks than the eldar can usually muster. Yriel's squad, meanwhile, has the always desireable option of accessing D4 melee on the prince himself, plus can create a huge swing if the foe undercommits on dealing with them and they can Withdraw and Reinforce. Don't sleep on the option of using the -2" charge stratagem to increase the chances of that either - that can be a big spanner in the works for melee enemies.

The Avatar and Eldrad round things out, the former forcing even more caution from foes thanks to the risk of him suddenly zooming 18" and Charging, while Eldrad keeps the army supplied with the copious quantities of CP it needs to power all the nonsense. Completely different to almost anything else out there, and super cool, congratulations Rhys!

Archetype

Board Control Cohort²

Thoughts

Double Cohort fun makes it to Japan, but with a more board presence-focused setup than the standard gunline option. The Robots still provide a central wrecking ball to oblierate foes, but surrounding them are lots of small Skitarii units with transports, ideal for grabbing objectives, a big Ruststalker squad as a melee threat (great with access to Advance/Charge from Thulia), and some back-filled anti-hull capability from Fusiliers. These are a proper steal at 140pts base, especially as the list can have both squads double Doctrinaed for maximum re-rolls if necessary. If opponents use the wrong tools to crack back, Analytical Reprisals can also be a huge blowout from them. I like the more balanced feel of this setup, even if the sheer brutality of the standard builds is hard to beat, and congratulations OZ on the triumph!

Analysis

The winning team brings together a pretty cool mix of lists, with a few specific synergies to call out. The list uses the sixes format to ensure that even after putting down its first Defender, it can have access to two pairs of builds with shared attributes, which can really limit what foes can safely defend with. The Knights and Orks can both go hard over the top shooting-wise, especially into hull-centric builds, while if enemies cannot handle a big unit of quality Terminators backed by a Primarch, both the Dark Angels and Thousand Sons can bully them. There's even a third sub-theme which is builds where all the key pieces are hulls/monsters, seen across all of the Necrons, World Eaters, Orks and Knights, creating a really uphill challenge for any composition without enough anti-tank.

That should ensure the team gets at least some very favourable matchups each round, and my instinct from some of the details of the lists is that the plan on paper was to set up 2 very favourable games in each round, and then hold the line with the rest. I say on paper because they obviously did way better than that, but several of these lists are very good at conserving points. Triple spawn in Thousand Sons maximises their PA capability, helping them eke out one more turn of scoring if things go south, while running shooty Orks as your Disruption choice is a great way to minimise the bleed on that Disposition. I also really like the use of Khorne Daemonkin for Reconnaisance - the Angron/Defiler/Skarbrand triumverate is so terrifying that foes can't go for a counterplay option of trying to rush down the army till they're dealt with, guaranteeing at least a few turns of free reign on scoring.

About the only thing here I'm not sold on is Inner Circle Task Force as a pair with Wrath instead of Assault Brethren. It has some cool tricks, but opening up a vulnerability to massed AP-1 weaponry (as Wrath doesn't get AoC) seems unnecessary, especially as the role of that build feels more like "don't die" than "do damage". Nitpick though - this setup seems really good, and earned a well-deserved win for the team, congratulations!

Analysis

A very different setup in second place, overlapping mainly on Necrons (and some similarity with the Ork build), but taking a different tack elsewhere. Here there's a significant pressure theme going on - both the Chaos lists do a bang up job of overwhelming the foe with mid-weight melee, and with Rigs in the Orks and double C'tan in the Necrons, both those builds can just roll some foes as well.

The GSC showcase a different spin on how to punish foes for trying to chase down Recon - counterattack potential. Big Neophyte squads with the Final Day and Xenocult buffs are extremely dangerous, and the enemy will need to be exquisitely careful about how much and where they commit against the army. Lots of Ingress threats there also really punishes low drop count builds. Disposition-wise, using Orks for Priority Assets is also interesting, as it isn't usually one of their frontrunners, but here I'd guess the thinking is that anything with the volume to chew through the pesty Grots is likely very vulnerable to a Meganob counterattack, letting the list pivot to a fairly defensive/counterpunch game plan if it finds itself facing the wrong targets.

Finally, the build I haven't mentioned yet is the Ultrawatch, mostly because they're in the classic position of being the best current singles build, and thus an easy include. You can drop them in anywhere! This is another great set of lists, well done to the team on second place.
